why_selected: Showed the Bakr tribes that Persian forces could be beaten once the Lakhmids were gone
Cost Rome its granary; the free bread ration of Constantinople ended in 618 as Egypt was lost
Ended the war and began four years of Sasanian civil war with some ten claimants

h: Yazdegerd III crowned; civil war ends
why_selected: A boy king on a throne the war had emptied, the year the Arab armies were organised under the first caliph

h: Arabs destroy the Sasanian army at Qadisiyyah
why_selected: Opened lower Iraq, the Sasanians' richest province; the commander Rostam Farrokhzad was killed
The capital fell after a three-month siege; the court fled to the Zagros
End of the Sasanian dynasty and of Iranian imperial independence for nearly two centuries

h: Tang China backs the Sasanian heir
why_selected: The last Sasanian appeal for outside help; the Tang title was nominal and Peroz died at the Tang court around 678
Veterans' pensions moved from generals' promises to a state fund fed by the first direct tax on citizens since 167 BCE
At the first succession the legions struck over pay and length of service; the price of the bargain made visible

h: Tiberius halts conquest beyond the Rhine
why_selected: Recall of Germanicus after three costly campaigns fixed the Rhine as the frontier for four centuries
First emperor chosen by soldiers; his donative of 15,000 sesterces a man set the price of later accessions
A conquest for prestige that tied down four legions, about an eighth of the army, on a province that never paid for them
First reduction of the imperial silver coin, to 1/96 of a pound; the start of the long debasement that paid the army
First civil war of the empire, decided by provincial armies; showed an emperor could be made away from Rome

h: Domitian raises army pay by a third
why_selected: First rise in legionary pay since Augustus, to 300 denarii; the army's claim on revenue ratcheted upward from here
Adoption of a frontier general gave four successions without civil war from 98 to 161
Last large conquest that paid for itself, in Dacian royal gold and the mines of Alburnus Maior

h: Hadrian begins his wall in Britain
why_selected: The plainest statement of the fixed-frontier policy: the empire defended what its taxes could pay for

h: Marcomannic Wars break the Danube line
why_selected: Germanic coalitions crossed the Danube and besieged Aquileia in 170, the first invasion of Italy in nearly three centuries

h: Commodus makes peace on the Danube
why_selected: End of the adoptive succession; his murder in 192 left no heir and opened the throne to the armies

h: Severus seizes Rome with the Danube legions
why_selected: After the Guard sold the throne, a frontier army took it; founded a dynasty that rested openly on the soldiers

h: Severus raises pay and lets soldiers marry
why_selected: Pay rose from 300 to 400 denarii while the denarius fell to about half silver; the army's cost outran the mines
Citizenship for nearly all free inhabitants, which widened the base of the inheritance tax that paid veterans
A 'double denarius' with about 1.5 denarii of silver; the coin whose collapse marks the third-century crisis

h: Plague of Cyprian spreads from Egypt
why_selected: A second pandemic that cut recruits and taxpayers in the worst decades of the crisis

h: Goths kill Emperor Decius at Abritus
why_selected: First Roman emperor killed in battle by a foreign enemy; the Danube line no longer held
The Rhine army made its own emperor to defend a frontier the centre could not reach; held Gaul and Britain until 274
An eastern client state turned rival took the empire's granary; Aurelian destroyed it in 272-273

h: Aurelian walls the city of Rome
why_selected: Rome's first new circuit wall since the fourth century BCE; the frontier no longer protected the core
First permanent surrender of a province; shortened the Danube line to free troops
Danubian soldier-emperor ended the Gallic and Palmyrene breakaways and tried to restore the coin
Four rulers with four armies, so that every frontier had an emperor near enough to stop a usurper
Tax assessed on fixed units of land and labour and collected largely in kind; freed the army's supply from the failed coin
Price caps on over a thousand goods, on pain of death, ignored within years; evidence of inflation the reforms could not stop
Soldiers' choice of a dead emperor's son broke the tetrarchic succession and began 18 years of civil war
Gold coin at 72 to the pound that held its standard for seven centuries; the late empire paid and taxed in it
Ended the tetrarchy's civil wars with one emperor, who chose the site across the strait for his new capital

h: Theodosius settles the Goths as federates
why_selected: First settlement of an autonomous armed people inside the empire under its own leaders; the model for the West's dismemberment
Last reunification of the whole empire under one ruler, won with Gothic federates who took the heaviest losses
Permanent split into eastern and western courts that competed for the Balkans and for the Goths' service

h: Vandals, Alans and Suebi cross the Rhine
why_selected: Began the loss of the western provinces' taxes: Gaul plundered, Britain cut off, Spain overrun by 409
Purge of the West's commander and massacre of federate soldiers' families sent perhaps 30,000 men to Alaric

h: Rome leaves Britain to its own defence
why_selected: First western diocese given up; its garrison had already left with the usurper Constantine III in 407
The barrier that kept invaders out of the East's tax base in Anatolia, Syria and Egypt; never breached until 1453
An army bought with a province: the first of the barbarian kingdoms carved from western taxpaying land
About 80,000 Vandals and Alans crossed from Spain to the one western region still untouched and paying

h: West admits it cannot pay its army
why_selected: Laws of Valentinian III conceding there was not enough revenue to feed new recruits; new sales tax and an end to exemptions
Forced the peace of 448 and a tribute of 2,100 pounds of gold a year; the Huns drained the East's surplus
The West's last great field victory, won with Visigothic allies while Africa stayed lost

h: Attila dies and his empire breaks up
why_selected: Release of the subject Germanic peoples after Nedao (454) and the end of the Hun auxiliaries the West had relied on
Gaiseric's fleet from Carthage plundered Rome for two weeks after Valentinian III's murder ended the Theodosian line in the West

h: Roman armada against the Vandals destroyed
why_selected: Last joint East-West attempt to recover Africa's revenue; its failure left the West without a fiscal base
Ostrogothic kingdom that kept the Roman tax system and Senate running in Italy under a Gothic army
Sound bronze coinage and taxes commuted to gold; left a treasury of 320,000 pounds of gold in 518
Riot against Justinian's tax ministers ended with some 30,000 killed; the regime came out free to spend on war
Close of a twenty-year war that left Italy poorer than the Goths had found it and too weak to hold
Within a decade most of Justinian's Italy was lost; Rome and Ravenna became outposts
Fall of the key Danube fortress opened the Balkans to Avar raids and Slav settlement
Coup from Carthage that put in power the emperor who would lose the east twice and win it back once
Walls and fleet kept the Avar and Persian armies apart; the capital's survival made the counter-offensive possible

h: Western Turks join Heraclius at Tiflis
why_selected: Steppe alliance arranged in 625 that opened a second front in the Caucasus and freed Heraclius to strike south

h: Khosrow II overthrown; Persia sues for peace
why_selected: Restored the old frontier and began four years of Persian succession struggles just before the Arab attack

h: Arabs destroy the Roman army at Yarmuk
why_selected: Loss of the eastern field army Heraclius had rebuilt; Syria abandoned
Loss of the richest province and its grain; what remained of the empire had to rebuild its army on Anatolian land

h: Rome defeats the Latins at Lake Regillus
why_selected: The young Republic's victory over the Latin cities that led straight to the treaty on which Rome built its alliances
The soldiers' strike that created the tribunate and opened two centuries of the Conflict of the Orders

h: Rome and Latins sign the Foedus Cassianum
why_selected: Mutual defence, equal booty and joint colonies: the template for the alliance system that conquered Italy
Rome's first written law, published on demand of the plebs; the root of the Roman legal tradition
Repealed the Twelve Tables' marriage ban; the first step toward a single patrician-plebeian nobility
Doubled Roman territory and gave plebeians land; Rome's first conquest of a major Etruscan city

h: Gauls win at the Allia, sack Rome
why_selected: The only sack of Rome for 800 years; drove fortification, colonisation and the reassertion of control over the Latins

h: Rome builds its stone circuit wall
why_selected: The 11 km wall of Veientine tufa built after the Gallic sack; Rome was never again taken by an Italian enemy

h: Licinian-Sextian laws open the consulship to plebeians
why_selected: Fused the patrician and plebeian elites into one nobility competing for command, the engine of expansion
The Latin cities' last bid for equal partnership, which Rome answered by dismantling their league
Graded citizenship and bilateral alliances: the settlement that turned defeated enemies into Roman manpower

h: Samnites trap a Roman army at Caudium
why_selected: Rome's worst humiliation of the Samnite Wars; spurred the roads, colonies and reforms that won them

h: Censor Appius Claudius builds the Via Appia
why_selected: The first great Roman military road, built to move legions to the Samnite front

h: Rome breaks the Italian coalition at Sentinum
why_selected: Rome defeated Samnites, Gauls, Etruscans and Umbrians together; decided the mastery of central Italy
Made plebiscites law for all citizens and ended the Conflict of the Orders; the legal basis of the Gracchi's tribunates
The first clash of legion and Hellenistic phalanx; the test of whether Rome's alliance would hold under defeat
Ended Pyrrhus's Italian war; a Hellenistic king beaten by Rome's capacity to replace its losses

h: Tarentum surrenders; Rome holds the south
why_selected: Completed Rome's control of the peninsula south of the Po and brought it to the Strait of Messina, facing Carthage

h: Rome's new fleet wins at Mylae
why_selected: Rome's first naval victory, won with the corvus by a state that had no war fleet four years earlier

h: Carthage cedes Sicily, Rome's first province
why_selected: The Aegates victory ended the First Punic War; Sicily became the first overseas territory Rome governed
Taken from Carthage during its mercenary war; the grievance that drove the Barcids to Spain

h: Hamilcar Barca begins Carthage's conquest of Spain
why_selected: Silver mines and Iberian soldiers rebuilt Carthaginian power and gave Hannibal his base

h: Hannibal crosses the Alps into Italy
why_selected: Carried the Second Punic War into Italy to break Rome's alliance system at its source

h: Hannibal ambushes a Roman army at Trasimene
why_selected: The largest ambush in Roman history; prompted Fabius Maximus's strategy of delay
Seized Carthage's Spanish capital, treasury and hostages; began the end of Barcid Spain

h: Rome destroys Hasdrubal's army at the Metaurus
why_selected: Stopped the reinforcement Hannibal needed; the war in Italy was lost for Carthage from here
Ended the Second Punic War; the treaty of 201 left Rome the only power in the western Mediterranean

h: Rome organises two provinces in Spain
why_selected: Committed Rome to seventy years of Spanish war and permanent overseas garrisons

h: Treaty of Apamea strips the Seleucids
why_selected: 15,000 talents and Asia Minor lost; built up Pergamum, whose king would later leave it to Rome

h: Rome creates a court for governors' extortion
why_selected: The first standing criminal court; its juries became the central prize of late-Republican politics
Ended the Celtiberian wars whose long service drained Italy's farmer-soldiers

h: Attalus III leaves Pergamum to Rome
why_selected: Rome's richest province, the province of Asia; its revenue became a weapon in Roman politics from the first year
The plantation economy built on war captives turned on its owners

h: Senate's emergency decree kills Gaius Gracchus
why_selected: The first senatus consultum ultimum: legalised killing of citizens as an instrument of politics

h: Rome declares war on Jugurtha of Numidia
why_selected: Exposed senatorial corruption and gave Marius the command that made him

h: Marius elected consul, enrols the propertyless
why_selected: A new man's consulship won against the nobility; later read as the start of a professional, general-loyal army

h: Cimbri and Teutones destroy two Roman armies
why_selected: Rome's worst defeat since Cannae; the emergency that justified Marius's five consecutive consulships

h: Marius destroys the Cimbri at Vercellae
why_selected: Ended the northern invasions and left Marius with veterans to settle

h: Saturninus killed under the emergency decree
why_selected: Veteran land and street violence fused; Marius enforced the decree against his own ally

h: Tribune Drusus assassinated over Italian citizenship
why_selected: Killing of the last reformer to offer the allies citizenship peacefully; the trigger for the Social War
Italy fought Rome for a share of its empire; ended with citizenship for all Italians south of the Po

h: Rome grants citizenship to loyal Italians
why_selected: More than doubled the citizen body; the distribution of the new citizens in the tribes caused the next crisis
Created the eastern command that Sulla and Marius fought over

h: Sulla marches his army on Rome
why_selected: The first Roman army to take Rome; the precedent for every civil war that followed

h: Cinna and Marius retake Rome by force
why_selected: The second march on Rome in two years; made civil war the routine settlement of political disputes

h: Sulla wins at the Colline Gate
why_selected: Decided Sulla's civil war against the Marians and Samnites at the walls of Rome

h: Sulla named dictator, proscribes his enemies
why_selected: Dictatorship without term, legal murder by list, and a Senate-first constitution that lasted a decade

h: Pompey and Crassus consuls; tribunes restored
why_selected: Two generals with armies at the gates took the consulship and dismantled Sulla's restrictions

h: Lex Gabinia gives Pompey the whole sea
why_selected: The model extraordinary command: one man, multi-year, empire-wide authority voted by the assembly
Executions of citizens without trial under the emergency decree; the act that later exiled Cicero

h: Pompey, Crassus and Caesar form a compact
why_selected: A private alliance that ran the state through the assembly over the Senate and gave Caesar Gaul
A consular, the Senate's voice, removed by a tribune's law with the triumvirs' consent
Turned a provincial governorship into an eight-year war of conquest

h: Triumvirs renew their compact at Luca
why_selected: Divided the empire's armies among three men for five more years

h: Clodius killed; Pompey made sole consul
why_selected: Gang war in the capital and the senate house burned; Pompey drew closer to the Senate against Caesar
Ended Gallic independence and gave Caesar a veteran army loyal to him alone
Decided the civil war; Pompey fled to Egypt and was killed on landing

h: Caesar crushes the last Pompeians at Munda
why_selected: Last battle of Caesar's civil war; left him without an armed rival
The attempt to restore the Republic by killing the dictator; reopened the civil wars

h: Antony, Octavian and Lepidus made triumvirs
why_selected: A legal dictatorship of three, with proscriptions to fund the legions
The Republic's leading civilian voice killed on the triumvirs' list

h: Antony and Octavian win at Philippi
why_selected: Ended the republican cause in arms; Brutus and Cassius killed themselves

h: Agrippa defeats Sextus Pompeius at Naulochus
why_selected: Secured the West and Italy's grain supply for Octavian; Lepidus removed the same year

h: Octavian takes Egypt as his own province
why_selected: Ended the last Hellenistic kingdom; Egypt's grain and treasure answered to the emperor alone
